News global nation business lifestyle entertainment technology sports opinion LATEST NEWS STORIES HEADLINES METRO REGIONS NATION WORLD CDN NEWSLETTER www / West Philippine Sea West Philippine Sea Tarriela likens sea violators to ‘Voldemort,’ Chinese scholar fires back By: Gabryelle Dumalag - @inquirerdotnet INQUIRER.net / 03:05 PM November 17, 2026 Share: MANILA, Philippines — Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela’s comparison of South China Sea law violators to the fictional Harry Potter series villain “Voldemort” drew pushback from a Chinese scholar on Tuesday.
“Right now, the international community no longer hesitates to call out who is Voldemort, who is aggressor, who is the victim, and who is the bozo,” Tarriela said during the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea in Parañaque City.
READ: Tarriela rebuffs Chinese scholar’s Ayungin shoal claim
Tarriela said the government’s transparency initiative had encouraged foreign governments to openly identify those responsible for aggressive actions at sea, unlike in previous years when they avoided naming the countries involved.
He compared their previous reluctance to identify maritime aggressors to the fear of mentioning Voldemort, whose name characters in the Harry Potter series avoided saying.
“Voldemort is so powerful that they cannot even mention his name,” he said.
Sophie Wushuang Yi of the Beijing-based Grandview Institution challenged Tarriela’s analogy, saying she was saddened by the comparison.
READ: Tarriela: Chinese envoy got the wrong Teodoro in oil talks row
“I’m really saddened to hear the comparison between Voldemort or you know who,” said Yi, a longtime Harry Potter fan who spent 11 years in the United Kingdom.
She argued that countries have different interpretations of justice and fairness, suggesting that a figure considered a villain by one side could be viewed as a hero by another.
“One country’s defense is another’s offense. One’s Voldemort is perhaps one’s Dumbledore,” she said.
Tarriela, however, clarified that his analogy was not directed exclusively at China but applied to any country violating international law.
“Those who violate the international law is Voldemort,” he said.
Yi also cited Beijing’s concerns over military exercises involving the US, the Philippines and Japan, saying such activities could be perceived as threatening by China even when participating countries considered them defensive.
She warned that intensifying military competition could increase the risk of unintended confrontations in the region.
“I sincerely hope that the existing diplomatic channels or the diplomatic dramas will not affect the existing communication channels that we have at the operational level,” Yi said.
Tarriela, meanwhile, rejected claims that the transparency initiative had escalated tensions in the South China Sea, saying it aimed to raise public awareness, encourage international support and counter misinformation.
“Transparency, it is not intended to provoke anybody,” he said.
The initiative began after a Chinese Coast Guard vessel directed a military-grade laser at BRP Malapascua, a Philippine patrol vessel, near Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in February 2023, shortly after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s state visit to Beijing.
Yi, meanwhile, called for “strategic empathy,” or understanding how another country interprets its actions without necessarily agreeing with its position.
